statements: The chief complaint is a 2-month history of sore throat, cough, hoarseness, and marked 10-kg weight loss.
The patient’s main concern is an upper aerodigestive/laryngeal process causing persistent throat symptoms plus systemic weight loss.
The patient has chronic immunosuppression from prednisone 15 mg/day for 5 years.
The patient is also taking hydroxychloroquine.
The patient has stage II pulmonary sarcoidosis.
Laryngoscopy showed multifocal supraglottic mucosal disease.
Laryngoscopy showed a centimetric polylobulated lesion on the free border of the epiglottis.
Laryngoscopy showed additional tiny lesions on the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis.
Laryngoscopy showed a small ulcerated area on the right arytenoid mucosa.
Vocal-fold and arytenoid motility are preserved.
The neck exam is normal.
The preserved vocal-fold and arytenoid motility and normal neck exam argue against bulky invasive laryngeal cancer with regional spread.
MRI showed only a small low-enhanced epiglottic lesion.
MRI showed no other laryngeal enhancement.
The MRI findings suggest superficial mucosal rather than deeply infiltrative disease.
PET-CT showed multiple ground-glass lung masses.
PET-CT showed bilateral nodules increased from prior imaging.
The PET-CT findings indicate active pulmonary pathology beyond a stable baseline sarcoidosis pattern.
The CBC is normal.
The metabolic panel is normal.
There are no neck masses.
There is no impaired laryngeal mobility.
The patient is a never-smoker.
Never-smoking lowers but does not eliminate the likelihood of primary laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma.
The absence of a neck mass and preserved mobility make advanced laryngeal malignancy less likely.
Normal routine labs do not strongly support a severe bacterial infection or hematologic malignancy.
The lesions are multifocal.
The lesions include ulceration.
The multifocal lesions and ulceration broaden consideration to inflammatory, granulomatous, infectious, and neoplastic causes.
The first major differential is laryngeal carcinoma.
Hoarseness, sore throat, weight loss, and an epiglottic lesion are compatible with supraglottic cancer.
Prior breast cancer raises concern for malignancy in general.
She is a never-smoker.
The neck exam is normal.
Vocal-fold and arytenoid motility is preserved.
MRI shows only a small low-enhanced lesion without broader infiltrative enhancement.
The laryngoscopic pattern is multifocal with tiny additional lesions and ulceration rather than a single dominant invasive mass.
Pulmonary PET-CT findings of multiple ground-glass masses and bilateral nodules are not the classic pattern for primary laryngeal cancer metastasis.
The second differential is laryngeal sarcoidosis.
She has known pulmonary sarcoidosis.
Sarcoidosis can involve the supraglottis, especially the epiglottis.
Sarcoidosis could explain epiglottic lesions and hoarseness.
She has been on long-term prednisone and hydroxychloroquine.
Long-term prednisone and hydroxychloroquine would usually suppress sarcoid activity.
The lesion description includes ulceration and multifocal mucosal lesions.
Ulceration and multifocal mucosal lesions are less typical than diffuse edematous supraglottic swelling.
The concurrent worsening pulmonary imaging with ground-glass masses and nodules in an immunosuppressed patient raises concern for opportunistic infection rather than simple sarcoid progression.
The third differential is laryngeal tuberculosis or another granulomatous infection.
Weight loss, cough, laryngeal ulcerative lesions, and pulmonary abnormalities could fit TB.
The pulmonary imaging described as multiple ground-glass masses and bilateral nodules is not specifically classic for TB.
There is no mention of fever, night sweats, hemoptysis, or epidemiologic risk factors.
TB remains plausible but not the best fit from the provided data.
A fourth and stronger differential is laryngeal fungal infection, particularly cryptococcosis.
Chronic corticosteroid use is a major risk factor for opportunistic fungal infection.
Laryngeal cryptococcosis can present with sore throat and hoarseness.
Laryngeal cryptococcosis often mimics laryngeal cancer on endoscopy with polypoid or ulcerative supraglottic lesions.
Pulmonary cryptococcosis can produce nodules or mass-like/ground-glass lesions.
The pulmonary cryptococcosis pattern fits the PET-CT description of multiple ground-glass lung masses and bilateral nodules.
The multifocal superficial laryngeal lesions, low-enhancement small lesion on MRI, normal neck exam, and preserved laryngeal mobility all favor an infectious mucosal process over invasive cancer.
In an immunosuppressed patient with worsening pulmonary lesions and laryngeal involvement, disseminated or concomitant pulmonary-laryngeal cryptococcosis is the most coherent explanation.

The combination of long-term prednisone exposure, multifocal supraglottic polylobulated/ulcerative lesions, constitutional weight loss, cough, and worsening pulmonary nodular/ground-glass lesions most strongly supports laryngeal cryptococcosis with pulmonary involvement rather than malignancy or sarcoid flare.
Among fungal causes, cryptococcosis is especially known to mimic laryngeal carcinoma.
Among fungal causes, cryptococcosis is especially known to occur in steroid-treated patients.
The single most likely diagnosis is laryngeal cryptococcosis.
Laryngeal cryptococcosis is a high-probability differential diagnosis.
Supraglottic laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma is a medium-probability differential diagnosis.
Laryngeal sarcoidosis is a medium-probability differential diagnosis.
Laryngeal tuberculosis is a low-probability differential diagnosis.
The final diagnosis is laryngeal cryptococcosis.
